raw: A B S T R A C T

text: Organic additives play an important role in regulating fi lm growth and properties in Cu electrodeposition. 3‑Mercapto‑1‑propane sulfonate (MPS) and its dimer bis(3‑sulfopropyl) disulfide (SPS) are representative accelerators that promote Cu electrodeposition rate. In this study, the formal reduction potential of SPS to MPS wa determined by measuring the equilibrium constants of thiol–disulfide interchange reactions with the reference thiol/disul fi de pairs by 1 H nuclear magnetic resonance (1H NMR) spectroscopy. The calculated formal reduction potential of SPS to MPS was 0.153 V (vs. standard hydrogen electrode). Based on this calculation, the cell potentials of Cu(I)(thiolate) formation reaction with either SPS or MPS, which is a key reaction in accelerating mechanism, were also estimated by ultraviolet–visible absorption and 1 H NMR spectroscopies: they were found to be 0.202 V and 0.214 V for SPS and MPS, respectively. The positive cell potential indicates that the formation of Cu(I)(thiolate) complexes is thermodynamically favorable in the presence of additives.

raw: 1. Introduction

text: Cu has been widely used as metallization material in the semi conductor industry owing to its low electrical resistivity and high electromigration resistance. Cu metallization is usually performed by electrodeposition, which e fi ciently yields high quality fi lms by a relatively simple and inexpensive process. Electrolyte for Cu electrodeposition typically contains small quantities of organic additives, which are essential to regulate fi lm growth and properties. Additives are grouped into accelerators, suppressors, and levelers according to their roles in controlling the deposition rate. Among them, 3‑mercap to‑1‑propanesulfonate (MPS) and its dimer bis(3‑sulfopropyl) disulfide (SPS) are the most representative accelerators in Cu electrodeposition [1].

One describes competitive adsorption between accel erator and suppressor; the displacement of suppressor inhibition layer by SPS or MPS facilitates the approach of Cu ions to electrode surface, enhancing the deposition rate [ 3 - 7 ]. The other mechanism focuses on direct catalytic reduction of Cu ^ 2 + ion to C u ^ + ion by forming Cu(I) (thiolate) complex [8–11]. The reduction of Cu ^ 2 + to Cu ^ + is known as the rate-determining step of Cu electrodeposition [12]. Vereecken et al. reported that the amount of C u ^ + near electrode surface is a key factor determining the deposition rate in Cu electrodeposition [13,14].

text: In the conventional CuSO –based Cu electrodeposition solution, major Cu species in the electrolyte is Cu ^ 2 +, not C u ^ +. At this situation, there are two possible mechanisms for the formation of Cu(I)(thiolate) in the presence of SPS. One is that SPS is reduced to MPS and then reacts with Cu ^ 2 + +. text: The formal reduction potential of SPS was fi rst determined by using thiol–disulfide interchange reaction with ME and Lip. The calculated formal reduction potential of SPS under the standard condition was 0.153 V (vs. SHE) in aqueous solution. The cell potential of the formation of Cu(I)(thiolate) complexes, which is the key reaction to explain the accelerating mechanism, was also estimated based on the formal reduction potential of SPS. The cell potential of Cu(I)(thiolate) formation between C u ^ + and SPS was 0.202 V, and the reaction between Cu ^ 2 + and MPS was 0.214 V. We believe that the thermodynamic values obtained in this study would be helpful in understanding or developing industrial Cu electrodeposition involving SPS.
